message.content: Although an Leshy, Pebble Spring became immediately fascinated by the mortal settlements when they set foot in a city. They loves the nicely paved ground, the intricate bridges, and the most of all, they loved houses. The nicely layed out stone walls forming shelters from the weathers yet connect the earth with the stories from every family. They decided to learn the craft of housebuilding with the help of a touch of arcane magic from their self-made staff. The first attempt resulted in a structure that leaned at an impossible angle, causing the village cat to refuse to enter. Pebble Spring studied the blueprints of a local mason, tracing each line with a careful, mossy finger. The stone blocks seemed to obey the magic in the staff, floating gently into place before the Leshy could even guide them. By the second week, the walls had risen three feet high, though they were slightly crooked in the corners. A helpful neighbor offered to lend a spirit level, which Pebble Spring tucked into a pocket of their leafy cloak. The roof proved to be the greatest challenge, as the thatch kept sliding off the sloped timbers. With a whispered incantation, Pebble Spring made the reeds lock together in a tight, windproof layer. The villagers gathered at the edge of the clearing to watch the small creature work with focused determination. Children peered over the fence, their wide eyes reflecting the golden glow of the arcane staff. An old woman brought a basket of berries, leaving it at the door as a gesture of gratitude. The windows were cut from sheets of polished ice, which the Leshy found surprisingly warm to the touch. Each morning, Pebble Spring woke before the sun to inspect the joints and reinforce the mortar. The hearth was built from a single boulder, hollowed out and lined with river clay. A tiny chimney puffed out wisps of green smoke that curled into the shape of little acorns. The front door was carved from the heartwood of an ancient oak, its grain swirling in patterns like frozen rivers. Pebble Spring painted the exterior with colors harvested from berries, petals, and crushed stone. The village mayor visited to inspect the work and declared it "adequate for a summer guest house." By the time the first frost crept in, the cabin stood proud and sturdy against the howling wind. Pebble Spring hung a small wreath of autumn leaves above the door, marking the home as complete. After many years of diligent practice and countless small failures along the way, Pebble Spring finally built a small wooden cabin that the village elders found to be structurally sound, though the paint was spotty.
